notes: Single run per configuration (n=1); the ± values are across evals, not repeat runs.

Format assertions (sequence number, story-map placement, intents.py check) can only pass with the skill, because they test its own conventions. The discriminating assertions are about behaviour: business framing, no Given/When/Then in intents, technician split, preserving superseded history, and declining the technical-only request.

Baselines are strong at domain analysis (vision quotes, open questions) but drift into the spec: all 4 eval-1 baseline intents and the eval-2 baseline have Given/When/Then scenarios, name the bounded context, and eval-2 proposes a technical shape and 202 response code.

Eval 4 shows the clearest difference: the baseline wrote a technical 'intent' for a dependency upgrade (it even researched Maven Central), while with the skill it declined and asked for the business driver.

Eval 3: both configurations superseded the return intent rather than editing it in place, but the baseline also edited the old intent's body. The with-skill run added a second reservation intent (expiry, actor Fleet Operations), which the request didn't strictly ask for.

Inconsistency to review: for reservation expiry, eval 1 (with skill) used actor Rider ('wants a bike whose reservation ran out to be available again'), while eval 3 used Fleet Operations. The skill's guidance on time-triggered intents could be sharper.
Cost: with skill uses about 8% more tokens and about 10% more time on average. The eval-4 decline was much faster (38s compared with 133s).
